decision.quote:
The video recordings of the test phase were coded for the presence or absence of self-oriented
behavior and analyzed using a nonparametric, one-tailed binomial test with a threshold level set
at .60 based on findings indicating that more than 60% of children older than 20 months will
self-orient within this paradigm (see Amsterdam, 1972; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978, Lewis &
Brooks-Gunn, 1979).
decision.location: Method (Dependent Measure, Analysis, and Reliability), p. 4 (also Introduction, p. 2)
decision.reason: Independent inspection of both Broesch et al. (2010) and the full text of Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière (1996; Developmental Psychology, 32(2), 313–321, DOI 10.1037/0012-1649.32.2.313) positively establishes that Asendorpf et al. (1996) is not an empirically retested target finding. Regardless of citation location, Asendorpf et al. (1996) did not investigate the 18-to-24-month developmental emergence of mirror self-recognition (MSR) or pass rates beyond 20 months: they tested a single cross-sectional age slice of 18.2- to 18.9-month-old Munich infants (M = 18.6 months; plus reanalyzed 19-month-olds from Asendorpf & Baudonnière, 1993), chosen on the basis of Lewis & Brooks-Gunn’s (1979) prior 18-month median benchmark so that roughly half the sample would be recognizers (45% immediate recognizers in the classic linguistic rouge test), in order to test (1) whether MSR is associated with sustained synchronic imitation and social contingency awareness and (2) whether modeling doll-cleaning with a tissue and verbally prompting children to clean their face reduces ambiguous non-touching cases at 18.6 months (from 26% to 11%, increasing total recognizers to 61%, chi-square(2, N = 98) = 4.38, p = .11). Broesch et al. (2010) do not test synchronic imitation, contingency awareness, or doll-cleaning/tissue prompting, and instead test 18- to 72-month-olds (Experiment 1, M = 41.62 months) and 36- to 55-month-olds (Experiment 2, M = 44.2 months) on an unprompted nonlinguistic sticker mark test against the >60% (>20 months) and >70%–88% (24+ months) age-emergence benchmarks established by Amsterdam (1972; shipped row input_row_index 843) and the longitudinal/age-series studies (targets 3, 4, 5, and 6).

decision.quote:
In 2006, Bard et al. compared spontaneous and
prompted self-orienting behaviors of children in the mark test and reported that maternal prompt-
ing increased self-referential verbal labeling. Although no statistical tests were applied (n = 4),
these findings do suggest that verbal prompts may be needed to encourage self-referential behav-
ior and labeling (Bard et al., 2006).
decision.reason: In the Introduction (p. 2), Broesch et al. (2010) cite Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens (2006; Infancy, 9(2), 191–219, DOI 10.1207/s15327078in0902_6) among eight studies attributed with the 18-to-24-month Western MSR pass-rate finding (~50% at 18 months and >70% at 24 months), whereas in the General Discussion (p. 9) they describe Bard et al. (2006) in terms of an n = 4 comparison of spontaneous versus maternally prompted self-orienting and verbal self-labeling. The supplied original source record for Bard et al. (2006) contains only the primary author abstract (level: primary_author_abstract), which confirms that the article reports a primary study with human infants comparing developmental and comparative mark-test procedures and maternal scaffolding in addition to the prompting subanalysis, but does not provide the full-text methods, infant age range, or unprompted mark-directed pass rates by age. Without the full text of Bard et al. (2006), the available evidence cannot settle the precise unresolved question of whether Bard et al.’s primary human-infant study empirically established the 18-to-24-month spontaneous mark-directed pass-rate benchmark retested by Broesch et al. (2010) or only tested procedural/scaffolding variations.

corrected_value.authors: Nielsen, M., Dissanayake, C., & Kashima, Y.
corrected_value.title: A longitudinal investigation of self-other discrimination and the emergence of mirror self-recognition.

decision.quote:
Note that the mirror mark paradigm used in this study is a simplified, nonlinguistic version com-
pared to the original, in which the child is specifically asked who is in the mirror (Amsterdam, 1972).
This simplified mirror mark test is similar to the one used in other studies with Western children
(Nielsen & Dissanayake, 2003; Nielsen et al., 2003; Nielsen et al., 2006; Suddendorf et al., 2007).
decision.location: Method (General Procedure), p. 3 (also Introduction, p. 2; General Discussion, p. 9; References, p. 12)
decision.reason: Independent inspection of Broesch et al. (2010) and the full text of Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima (2003; Infant Behavior & Development, 26(2), 213–226, DOI 10.1016/s0163-6383(03)00018-3) confirms that Nielsen et al. (2003) is a primary empirical source of the 18-to-24-month Western MSR emergence finding retested across cultures by Broesch et al. (2010), not merely a method precedent. In Nielsen et al. (2003, Sections 2.4 and 3.2, pp. 217–221, Fig. 1), 98 predominantly Caucasian middle-class Melbourne infants were tested longitudinally every 3 months through 24 months (MSR tested at 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24 months) using the simplified nonlinguistic forehead-sticker mark test (surreptitiously placing a sticker at the forehead/fringe during toy play, followed by a pretest check and unprompted mirror exposure), finding a mean, median, and mode age of MSR emergence of 18 months (~65% cumulative pass rate by 18 months) and >90% (76 of 83 infants) passing by 24 months. Broesch et al. (2010) explicitly attribute this 18-to-24-month Western pass-rate benchmark (~50% by 18 months and >70% by 24 months) to Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima (2003) in the Introduction (p. 2), adopt the same simplified nonlinguistic forehead-sticker procedure in the Method section (p. 3, citing Nielsen et al., 2003), and retest whether high spontaneous pass rates on this version of the MSR test replicate across seven cultural groups in Experiments 1 and 2 (General Discussion, p. 9). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 843, Amsterdam 1972, DOI 10.1002/dev.420050403) and sibling missing targets (Bertenthal & Fisher 1978, Lewis & Brooks-Gunn 1979, Lewis & Ramsay 2004) are separate studies by different author teams in different decades, so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Abrams, D., Wetherell, M., Cochrane, S., Hogg, M. A., & Turner, J. C.
corrected_value.title: Knowing what to think by knowing who you are: Self-categorisation and the nature of norm formation, conformity and group polarisation

decision.quote: Consistent with the assumption of the SCT (Turner, 1991;Turner et al., 1987), participants exposed to the in-group majority showed the increase in conformity in comparison to the standard condition in which group identity was not salient. On the opposite, when the majority was presented as the out-group, the conformity effect significantly dropped. Thus, we replicated and extended past research (Abrahams et al., 1990), showing that self-categorization could play a determining role in conformity even in more minimal conditions, in which salient in-and out-group characteristics (i.e., ethnicity) were completely irrelevant for the task at hand.
decision.location: Discussion, line 8 (also Introduction, lines 5–6; Results, lines 10–11; References, line 17)
decision.reason: The paper explicitly retests the empirical finding of Abrams, Wetherell, Cochrane, Hogg, and Turner (1990; British Journal of Social Psychology, 29(2), 97–119, DOI 10.1111/j.2044-8309.1990.tb00892.x; spelled Abrahams et al., 1990 in the Discussion) that self-categorization (in-group versus out-group majority membership) moderates judgmental conformity in the Asch line-judgment paradigm. In the Introduction (lines 5–6), the authors detail Abrams et al.’s (1990) experiment and explain that they adapted Abrams et al.’s (1990) design using ethnic in-group (Bosniak), out-group (Serb), and control (no salient group identity) five-confederate majorities (N = 76) to test group-similarity moderation without confounding similarity and task competence; in the Results (lines 10–11) and Discussion (line 8), they report a significant planned linear contrast between in-group and out-group majority conditions (F(1, 73) = 11.93, p < .001, eta_p^2 = .14; conformity M = 6.28 / 52.33% in-group vs. M = 4.24 / 35.31% control vs. M = 1.9 / 15.83% out-group) and explicitly state that they replicated and extended Abrams et al. (1990). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 7, Asch 1956, Psychological Monographs, DOI 10.1037/h0093718) is Solomon Asch’s 1956 baseline majority-conformity monograph without self-categorization conditions, a distinct work published 34 years earlier by a different author, so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Sonnenschein, R.; Kuemmerle, T.; Udelhoven, T.; Stellmes, M.; Hostert, P.
corrected_value.title: Differences in Landsat-Based Trend Analyses in Drylands due to the Choice of Vegetation Estimate.

decision.quote: Although not numerically comparable (due to several reasons discussed in Section 1.1), these numbers resemble the findings in Hostert et al. [42], who found that over 40% of the mountain area of central Crete (Psiloritis) showed a decreasing trend of vegetation cover. Spatial patterns are also very similar to the maps published by Sonnenschein et al. [49], both indicating that general reproducibility with the past papers is given from a thematic perspective with a focus on overgrazing and that similar conclusions would have been drawn as before.
decision.location: Results and Discussion (Comparison of Long-Term Vegetation Change), line 43 (also Case Study, line 7; Data, lines 12–14; Methods, lines 16 and 20; References [49])
decision.reason: The paper explicitly reproduces and replicates the empirical dryland vegetation trend analysis of Sonnenschein, Kuemmerle, Udelhoven, Stellmes, and Hostert (2011; Remote Sensing of Environment, 115(6), 1408–1420, DOI 10.1016/j.rse.2011.01.021, cited as [49]) alongside Hostert, Röder, and Hill (2003; [42]). Specifically, the authors adopt Sonnenschein et al.’s [49] 1984–2006 study period, CORINE 2006 semi-natural mask, and 14 manually selected Landsat TM/ETM+ acquisition dates (Table 2) to construct the static-selection baseline workflow (VD 1.0, [42,49]) and then replicate the long-term Crete vegetation trend analysis using all 2,816 available Landsat images and phenology-adaptive metrics (VD 2.0), directly comparing the spatial patterns and net cover trends (50% decline vs. 26% increase in VD 1.0 versus 18% decline vs. 50% increase in VD 2.0) against Sonnenschein et al. [49]. Although Patrick Hostert is a co-author on both papers, Sonnenschein et al. (2011) is a distinct empirical study published eight years after the sole shipped original (input_row_index 1191, Hostert, Röder, & Hill 2003, Remote Sensing of Environment, 87(2–3), 183–197, DOI 10.1016/s0034-4257(03)00145-7) that analyzed a different 1984–2006 TM/ETM+ dataset (excluding the 1977–1983 MSS data of Hostert et al. 2003 and adding 1997–2006 observations) to test sensitivity across vegetation estimates (NDVI, SAVI, SMA), so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.title: Seeking subjective dominance in multidimensional space: An explanation of the asymmetric dominance effect.

decision.quote:
This article reports two very close replication studies of the decoy effect, targeting

Experiment 1 in Ariely and Wallsten (1995) and Experiment 1 in Connolly et al. (2013).
decision.location: Introduction, p. 5 (also Abstract, p. 2; Study 1, pp. 12–28; General Discussion, p. 50; References, p. 59)
decision.reason: Study 1 of the article is an explicit, pre-registered direct replication of Experiment 1 in Ariely and Wallsten (1995; Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 63(3), 223–232, DOI 10.1006/obhd.1995.1075). Using N = 1,004 MTurk participants across five product categories (microwave ovens, running shoes, computers, televisions, and bicycles), Study 1 retests Ariely and Wallsten’s (1995) Experiment 1 finding (N = 76, F(1, 64) = 4.65, p < .05, d_z = 0.25) that adding an asymmetrically dominated decoy increases preference points allocated to the target option relative to the competitor, finding no overall decoy effect in the replication (t(1003) = -0.32, p = .624, d_z = -0.01; Study 1 Results and Discussion, pp. 19–28, Table 2). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 1586, Connolly, Reb, & Kausel 2013, Judgment and Decision Making, 8(2), 136–149, DOI 10.1017/s1930297500005064) is a separate original study on regret salience in job-choice sets that is independently replicated in Study 2, so report equivalence does not apply.
